# Cuts and wounds

Home care for the ordinary kitchen-knife, bike-fall and garden-tool injuries.

## Stopping the bleeding

Press firmly on the cut with a clean cloth for 10 minutes without peeking. Raise the injured part above the heart if you can. If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top rather than removing it. Call 911 if blood spurts, or if it has not slowed after 10 minutes of steady pressure.

## Cleaning a cut

Rinse under running water for several minutes. Wash around the wound with mild soap and keep soap out of it. Pat dry and cover with a clean bandage. Hydrogen peroxide and iodine can damage tissue and are not needed.

## When a cut needs stitches

See a doctor for a cut that gapes open, is deeper than about a quarter inch, is on the face or over a joint, or keeps bleeding. Stitches work best within 8 to 12 hours of the injury.

## Puncture wounds and tetanus

A nail, a fishhook or a bite can push germs deep. Let it bleed a little, rinse well, and check the date of your last tetanus shot: a booster is advised if it was more than 10 years ago, or more than 5 years ago for a dirty wound.

## Blisters from rubbing

A friction blister from a new shoe is best left alone: the roof of the blister is a sterile bandage. Cover it with a bandage or a donut-shaped pad. If it breaks, wash it, leave the skin flap in place, and cover it. Drain a large painful one only with a clean, sterilized needle.

## Signs of infection

Redness that spreads, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaks running up the limb, or a fever means the wound may be infected. See a doctor the same day.
